title: The desert, Luke's way (Luke 4:1–13)
hook: full of the Spirit, led into the wilderness, and the devil leaves until an opportune time

segments.voice: Yesterday, Luke's family tree, climbing back to Adam. Your line was son of adam, son of god. Did it change how you saw someone who annoyed you? Day five hundred fifteen.

Anyone who has quit something knows the dangerous moment isn't always the first day. It's day forty. You've made it. You're proud. You're tired. And then the old thing shows up, sounding perfectly reasonable. Luke's story of Jesus in the wilderness begins with a phrase worth noticing. In the King James Bible: "Jesus being full of the Holy Ghost returned from Jordan, and was led by the Spirit into the wilderness." Full of the Spirit, and led straight into the hardest place. Forty days without food. And Luke says, with almost comic plainness, "when they were ended, he afterward hungered." That's when the voice arrives.
screen: `FULL OF THE SPIRIT, LED INTO THE WILDERNESS.`

segments.voice: The devil makes three offers, and each one is aimed at something real. First, hunger: "If thou be the Son of God, command this stone that it be made bread." Jesus answers from Deuteronomy: "It is written, That man shall not live by bread alone, but by every word of God." Second, power: all the kingdoms of the world, shown in a moment, if he will only worship. He refuses. Third, Luke takes him to Jerusalem, to a high point of the temple: throw yourself down, the angels will catch you. And this time the devil quotes scripture too, a psalm about angels bearing you up. Jesus answers: "It is said, Thou shalt not tempt the Lord thy God." Here's Luke's way. Matthew tells the same three tests, but puts the mountain last. Luke puts Jerusalem last. That's no accident: Luke's whole Gospel walks toward Jerusalem. It opened there, with Zechariah in the temple, and it will end there. And then the line that gives today its name. "And when the devil had ended all the temptation, he departed from him for a season." The Greek is achri kairou, until an opportune time, until the right moment comes around again. Not gone forever. Just waiting. Luke doesn't pretend the desert was the last test. Readers often see the opportune time return near the end of the Gospel, when Luke says Satan entered into Judas, and in the garden, where Jesus prays in agony. Christians have long read this as honest news: passing one test doesn't end the testing. Temptation keeps a calendar.
screen: then, large: `HE DEPARTED FROM HIM FOR A SEASON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: know your weakest hour. Settle, and breathe. Everyone has one. Late at night with the phone. Right after a hard meeting. Sunday evening. The first hour home. Hungry, tired, alone, bored. Walk through an ordinary day in your mind and notice where you tend to slide into the thing you wish you didn't do. Don't scold yourself. Just find the hour, the way you'd find a weak board in a floor. Then think of one small thing to put there ahead of time: a glass of water, a walk, a verse, a friend to text, the phone in another room. If you pray, you can name that hour to God. If you don't, simply name it to yourself. The bell holds the time.
The desert. In Luke, Jesus goes in full of the Spirit, answers three tests with scripture, and the devil leaves only until an opportune time.
Your line: until another time. Today, when your weakest hour comes around, have the small thing ready, and notice that you saw it coming. Day five hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Many churches read the temptation in the wilderness on the first Sunday of Lent, and the forty days of Lent are often linked to Jesus' forty days in the desert.

original.note: Greek: the right time, the opportune moment. the devil leaves achri kairou, until such a time.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus beat temptation once, and that was that.
what it means: Luke says the devil left only for a season, and that honesty makes room for later tests.
what a scholar hears: Luke ends the tests at the temple in Jerusalem, the city his whole Gospel travels toward.
recall: Latin for magnify, the song's first word

notes: Greek achri kairou in 4:13 ('until an opportune time'). Confirm.
Linking the 'season' to Luke 22:3 (Satan entering Judas) is a common reading, framed as 'readers often see'. Confirm.
KJV 4:4 includes 'but by every word of God', which some manuscripts lack. The quote follows the KJV.
Did not quote 4:8 because the KJV wording ('Get thee behind me, Satan') is absent from many manuscripts; paraphrased instead.
